title: Discover
summary: Most expensive bugs are requirements bugs, not code bugs — I spend time scoping before I touch an editor, because a wrong assumption compounds with every hour spent building on top of it.

points.why: surfaces the real constraint before it becomes a rewrite
points.detail: talk directly to whoever hits the problem today; their workaround usually tells you more than the ticket does.

points.why: keeps the team from building the wrong thing, well
points.detail: restate the ask as the outcome that should change, not the feature that was requested.

points.why: a design that ignores timeline, team, or data constraints doesn't ship
points.detail: write down what's actually fixed — deadline, existing schema, headcount — before proposing anything.

points.why: gives "done" a testable definition on day one, not an argument on day thirty
points.detail: define the specific, verifiable conditions that prove the problem is solved, before writing any code.

example: On the event registration system, the original ask was "add a CSV export so admins can see who's registered." Talking to the admins who'd actually use it surfaced the real problem: the dashboard had no way to flag duplicate or conflicting registrations before an event, so they were catching those manually, after the fact, at check-in. The ticket became a real-time conflict view instead of an export button — a smaller build than requested, and the thing that actually fixed their recurring complaint.

title: Design
summary: I'd rather spend an afternoon on a design doc than a week unwinding a bad data model in production — most hard bugs are architecture decisions nobody wrote down.

points.why: forces trade-offs onto paper before they're load-bearing in code
points.detail: a short written proposal: the approach taken, the alternative considered, and why it lost.

points.why: lets frontend and backend build in parallel against a stable shape
points.detail: agree on request/response shapes before either side writes implementation code.

points.why: the cost of a wrong schema compounds with every row written against it
points.detail: model around how data is actually queried, not just how it's created.

points.why: keeps a team from re-implementing a problem someone already solved
points.detail: explicitly weigh consistency vs. availability, latency vs. simplicity, custom code vs. an existing library, before committing.

example: For the helpdesk management system, the key decision was how to model ticket ownership. The obvious approach — a single assigned_agent_id column on the ticket — was rejected because it couldn't represent reassignment or escalation history, which the support team needed for SLA auditing. Modeling assignment as its own table, separate from the ticket, cost one extra join on every read but meant escalations were just new rows, not destructive updates.

title: Build
summary: Shipping in small, reviewable pieces is the single habit that's saved me the most time — a 2,000-line pull request is a pull request nobody actually reviews.

points.why: a diff a reviewer can hold in their head catches more bugs than one they skim
points.detail: one logical change per pull request, not one feature spanning a dozen files.

points.why: catches a regression before a reviewer or a user does
points.detail: write the test for the behavior you just added in the same sitting, not as a follow-up ticket.

points.why: a second set of eyes catches the assumption you stopped noticing
points.detail: treat review comments as free bug reports, not as obstacles to merging.

points.why: decouples deploying code from releasing a feature
points.detail: ship the code dark, verify it in production, then flip it on — instead of a release day that's also the first real-world test.

example: Building checkout for the handmade-candle e-commerce site, I split what could've been one large "add checkout" change into separate pull requests — cart persistence, address capture, payment integration, order confirmation — each shippable on its own. That discipline paid off directly: a reviewer caught that a failed or cancelled payment wasn't handled before the order record was created, which would have left paid-looking orders in the database for carts that never actually completed.

title: Verify
summary: "It works on my machine" isn't verification — I only consider something done once I can see it behaving correctly in production, not just in a test suite.

points.why: catches different classes of bugs at the cheapest layer that can catch them
points.detail: most coverage from fast unit tests, fewer but real integration tests, a thin layer of end-to-end tests for the critical paths.

points.why: limits the blast radius of a bad change before it reaches every user
points.detail: roll out to a subset of traffic or a pre-production environment first, and watch it before a full release.

points.why: turns "it broke" into "here's exactly what broke and why"
points.detail: instrument logs, metrics, and traces so a production issue is diagnosable from a dashboard, not from guesswork.

points.why: makes a bad deploy a five-minute incident instead of a five-hour one
points.detail: know how to revert before you need to, not while an incident is already live.

example: On the event management system, the real test wasn't the staging environment — it was event day itself, a fixed deadline with a traffic spike right as doors opened. Rather than find out live, I load-tested the check-in flow specifically ahead of the event, which surfaced a slow query under concurrent check-ins that never showed up under normal day-to-day traffic. Fixed before the event, not during it.
